sentences.text:
Author: Rongon Mukhopadhyay Bench: Rongon Mukhopadhyay  Criminal Revision No. 259 of 2002  ---
 In the matter of an application under Sections 397 and 401 of the Code of  Criminal Procedure, 1973  ---
 Kali Podo Mandal S/o Futuk Mandal Resident of village Barbad,
 P.S. Tundi, District Dhanbad ... ... Petitioner  Versus  The State of Jharkhand ... ...

Opposite Party  ---
 For the Petitioner : None

For the Opp. Party : Mr. Rajnish Vardhan, A.P.P.
 ---
 Present:
 HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE RONGON MUKHOPADHYAY  ----
By Court:
No one appears on behalf of the petitioner.

However,
Mr. Rajnish Vardhan, learned A.P.P., is present.
Since this revision application is pending since 2002, the same is being disposed of based on the materials available on records.

This application is directed against the judgment dated 06.05.2002 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, IX, Dhanbad in Criminal Appeal No. 170 of 1994 whereby and whereunder the judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the learned S.D.J.M.,
Dhanbad in P.F. Case No. 44 of 1991 convicting the petitioner for the offence punishable under Section 16(i)(a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and sentencing him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months has been affirmed.
It appears that on 17.01.1990 the Food Inspector along with two officials witnesses had visited the shop of the petitioner and had purchased three packets of iodized salt.
Small contents from each of the packets were taken as sample and they were sent to the public analyst.
The public analyst submitted a report in which it was stated that the seized salt was adulterated.
After obtaining sanction for prosecution from the local authority P.F. Case No. 44 of 1991 was instituted.
The prosecution in course of its evidence had examined three witnesses.
P.W. - 1, Birendra Kumar Sinha, is the Food Inspector who had visited the shop of the petitioner and had purchased three packets of salt weighing one kilogram each.

He has further stated that three Kali Podo Mandal vs State Of Jharkhand on 10 April, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139963800/
1 packets of salt were wrapped separately and the paper which was affixed on it was signed by the petitioner and the purchase slip was also prepared.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This witness has further stated that one part of the sample was sent to the public analyst and the rest two packets were sent to the local health authority.
It has also stated by this witness that after the salt was found to be adulterated the sanction for prosecution was obtained from local authority and the prosecution report was filed.
P.W. - 1 has further stated that the report of the public analyst revealed that there was no iodine in the salt whereas the report of the Central Food Laboratory disclosed otherwise.
P.W. - 2, Kayum Ansari, was tendered by the prosecution.

P.W.- 3, Fagu Mian, is also said to have accompanied P.W. - 1 and he has also stated in similar terms to what has been stated by P.W.
- 1.
D.W. - 1, Adalat Gorain and D.W. - 2, Kalipada Mandal had stated that salt was seized from a gunny bag which was kept loose and sealed in bottles.
In the trial court a submission was advanced on behalf of the petitioner that the report of the public analyst as well as the report of the Central Food Laboratory contradicted each other.
A further submission had been advanced that Section 13 (2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act has been violated.
The learned trial court as well as the learned appellate court had appreciated the contentions made on behalf of the petitioner.

It appears that on 01.06.1991 the petitioner had surrendered before the trial court and on the same day had prayed that the seized sample be sent to the Central Food Laboratory for its examination which was allowed and accordingly the sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory and a report was also prepared which was exhibited.

Thus the contention of the petitioner that Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act was not complied, gets diluted in view of the right exercised by the petitioner in getting the sample tested by the Central Food Laboratory.

Although the report of the public analyst and the report of the Central Food Laboratory (Exhibits - 4 and 5) may have differed slightly with respect to the content of iodine in the salt but both the reports do suggest that iodized salt seized from the petitioner was adulterated.
Such circumstance, therefore, negates the contention which was raised by the petitioner before the learned courts below.

On proper appreciation of the evidence both oral and documentary on records the learned court below has rightly convicted the petitioner under Section 16(i)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
The learned appellate court has also on proper appreciation of the materials available on record affirmed the judgment and order of conviction.
There being no materials to conclude otherwise the conviction of the petitioner is, hereby, sustained.
However, with respect to the sentence which has been imposed upon the petitioner, it appears that the case was instituted in the year 1991.
The petitioner has been sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months.
The petitioner is facing the rigors of the prosecution case since last more than thirty five years.
Such circumstance, therefore, definitely entitles the petitioner for reconsideration of the quantum of sentence awarded to him.
In such view of the matter, the sentence imposed upon the petitioner is modified to the period already undergone.
